Empirical Research Plan – “Regulation and the High Cost of Housing in Manhattan”  

----------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy  
----------------------------------------------------
Method: Difference-in-Differences (DID) with an event-study (dynamic DID) specification.

Why appropriate?  
• We observe repeated cross-sections (or panels) of U.S. metropolitan areas over several decades.  
• Manhattan experienced discrete, well-dated tightenings of zoning/land-use regulations (e.g., 1961 Zoning Resolution; 1981 contextual down-zonings; mid-1990s historic-district expansion).  
• Other large metro counties did not adopt equally stringent reforms at the same moments; they supply a plausible counterfactual trend in the absence of the policy.  
• A DID/event-study compares the evolution of prices in Manhattan before/after each reform to the evolution in the control metros, while the event-study coefficients allow visual and formal tests of the parallel-trends assumption.

----------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control  
----------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
Treated = 1 if a county-year is subject to a “binding” regulatory tightening. We code a tightening when the Wharton Regulation Index (WRLURI) or alternatively the Zoning Floor-Area-Ratio (FAR) cap declines by ≥ x percent relative to the county’s pre-period mean.  
In Manhattan (New York County) key treatment years are 1961, 1981, and 1993.

Control group  
All other large central counties in the 25 largest U.S. MSAs that:  
(a) have WRLURI or FAR caps, but  
(b) did not change them by more than 5 percent in that same calendar year.  
E.g., Cook-IL (Chicago), Los Angeles-CA, King-WA (Seattle), etc.  
We will prune controls using synthetic-control weights or propensity-score re-weighting to improve pre-period balance.

Treatment timing  
Year t0 is the calendar year the new regulation became binding (1961, 1981, 1993 for Manhattan). Cities that never adopt are “never-treated.” If other cities adopt later, we will treat the design as staggered adoption and use Callaway-Sant’Anna / Sun-Abraham estimators.

----------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
----------------------------------------------------
A1 Parallel Trends: In the absence of regulation, Manhattan housing prices would have followed the same trend as the control group.  
Plausibility: Big “macro” shocks hit U.S. cities roughly similarly; still, NYC-specific finance booms may violate it. We will assess using 10-year pre-period event-study leads.

A2 No Anticipatory Effects: Prices do not jump in advance of the formal passage of the ordinance. For the 1961 reform, the first public draft was mid-1959; we will include leads to detect anticipation.

A3 Stable Unit Treatment Value (no spillovers): Regulatory changes in Manhattan do not directly affect, say, Chicago prices. Interstate spillovers are likely small; intra-NYC spillovers (e.g., to Brooklyn) motivate robustness checks that drop nearby counties.

A4 No time-varying composition: The set of housing units tracked in CPI data is stable or we can quality-adjust via hedonic indices.

----------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation  
----------------------------------------------------
T1 Policy endogeneity (regulation responds to rising prices).  
 – Mitigation: (i) Use pre-determined instruments for regulation intensity (share of landmarked lots pre-1910, Manhattan bedrock depth, % of parcels already overbuilt), or (ii) control for lagged price growth.  

T2 Non-parallel macro shocks (finance-sector booms concentrated in NYC).  
 – Mitigation: Add metro-specific linear time trends, interact year effects with census-division dummies, and perform a synthetic-control DID that explicitly balances pre-trends in GDP, employment composition.  

T3 Data mis-measurement of regulatory stringency.  
 – Mitigation: Cross-validate WRLURI with local FAR caps, down-zoning maps, and building-permit denials; instrument WRLURI with text-based counts of zoning-board appeals to create a plausibly exogenous proxy.

----------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline  
----------------------------------------------------
```
# 0. Packages ----------------------------------------------------------
library(tidyverse)     # data wrangling
library(fixest)        # fast fixed effects
library(haven)         # if Stata dta files exist
library(did)           # Callaway & Sant'Anna
library(bacondecomp)   # Goodman-Bacon weights

# 1. Load data ---------------------------------------------------------
price  <- read_csv("metro_price_index.csv")        # FHFA or CPI-converted
cost   <- read_csv("construction_costs.csv")
reg    <- read_csv("zoning_regulation_index.csv")  # WRLURI or FAR caps
controls <- read_csv("metro_controls.csv")         # pop, income, etc.

panel <- price %>%
  left_join(cost,    by = c("fips","year")) %>%
  left_join(reg,     by = c("fips","year")) %>%
  left_join(controls,by = c("fips","year"))

# 2. Variable construction --------------------------------------------
panel <- panel %>%
  mutate(treated =
           if_else(fips=="36061" &       # Manhattan FIPS
                   (year>=1961 | year>=1981 | year>=1993),1,0),
         post1961 = if_else(year>=1961,1,0),
         lnp      = log(hpi_nominal),
         lncc     = log(const_cost_index))

# 3. Two-way FE DID ----------------------------------------------------
did_basic <- feols(lnp ~ treated + lncc + pop + income_percap |
                     fips + year,
                   data = panel, cluster = ~fips)
summary(did_basic)

# 4. Event-study (Sun–Abraham) ----------------------------------------
panel <- panel %>%
  group_by(fips) %>%
  mutate(first_treat_year = min(if_else(treated==1, year, Inf))) %>%
  ungroup()

es_sa <- feols(lnp ~ sunab(first_treat_year, year) + lncc + pop + income_percap |
                 fips + year,
               data = panel, cluster = ~fips)
iplot(es_sa)     # pre-trend visualization

# 5. Robustness: Synthetic-control DID -------------------------------
library(augsynth)
syn_res <- augsynth(lnp ~ treated, fips, year, panel,
                    progfunc = "Ridge", scm = TRUE)
plot(syn_res)

# 6. Bacon decomposition (treatment-timing bias check) ---------------
bacondecomp(did_basic)

```
The code assumes long (fips×year) panel format and clusters at the metro (fips) level. Robustness checks include (i) adding metro-specific linear trends, (ii) synthetic-control balancing, and (iii) Goodman-Bacon decomposition to diagnose negative weights.

----------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results  
----------------------------------------------------
Theory (supply elasticity under regulatory constraint) predicts:  
A binding tightening raises the price of land and therefore housing. I expect Manhattan’s 1961 zoning to increase constant-quality housing prices by roughly 10–20 percent within five years and perhaps 30 percent after two decades, relative to the counterfactual path—comparable to the 15–35 percent estimates in Glaeser-Gyourko (2003) for Boston’s constraints. Construction costs should diverge far less, implying an expanding “regulation tax” wedge.

----------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID)  
----------------------------------------------------
C1 Pre-treatment parallel trends visually confirmed via event-study: 1  
C2 No differential anticipation: 0.5 (possible speculation in 1959–60)  
C3 No spillovers to controls: 1  
C4 No simultaneous confounders (city-specific demand shocks) after controls: 0.5  
C5 Consistency of treatment definition & timing across units: 1  

Overall score: 4 / 5 – credible but not bullet-proof; robustness and IV augmentations will be emphasized in the paper.
